scope: Selected primary studies; curated research map, not a systematic review or a clinical decision tool. Research only; not medical advice.

states.label: Functioning
states.description: A living dopaminergic neuron with established phenotype and activity. A reference concept, not a diagnostic baseline for individuals.
states.boundary: No single biomarker establishes whole-neuron health; functions change with context.

states.label: Function impaired
states.description: The neuron or its terminals may remain present while measured neurotransmission or related imaging signals are abnormal.
readouts: VMAT2 PET binding in human striatum
states.boundary: Reduced VMAT2 binding is not a cell count and cannot distinguish reversible regulation from terminal loss on its own.

states.label: Senescence-associated
states.description: A stress/inflammatory program resembling cellular senescence can appear in neurons, which are already mostly post-mitotic.
states.boundary: Neuronal senescence is not simply 'stopped dividing'. Marker expression alone cannot establish permanent or reversible senescence.

states.label: Neuron or terminal lost
states.description: Loss of cells or projections requires anatomical evidence and is biologically different from a change in molecular or imaging signal.
states.boundary: None of the studies in this R6 collection establishes progressive loss of dopamine neurons in people with long COVID.

studies.title: SARS-CoV-2 infection causes dopaminergic neuron senescence
studies.model: Human stem-cell-derived midbrain dopamine neurons, transplantation model and postmortem tissue
studies.observed: Human stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons were susceptible to infection in experimental settings and developed inflammatory and senescence-associated responses. Related signatures were detected in examined postmortem midbrain samples.
studies.notShown: This does not establish how commonly human dopamine neurons are infected in ordinary COVID, whether these changes are permanent, or that COVID causes Parkinson's disease.
studies.context: A drug screen identified riluzole, metformin and imatinib as hits under experimental conditions; no evidence of human treatment efficacy or neuron rejuvenation was established.
studies.disclosure: Review disclosures in the primary article; bench-screen hits are not treatment recommendations.

studies.title: Loss of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 in striatum of long COVID and relationship to neuropsychiatric symptoms
studies.model: Human case-control PET; 24 adults with long COVID and 24 matched controls (43 controls in exploratory comparison)
studies.observed: Striatal VMAT2 PET binding was lower in the long-COVID group; regional binding was associated with measures including apathy, motor slowing and exploratory memory findings.
studies.notShown: PET binding does not directly count living dopamine neurons or establish causation, direct viral brain infection, individual prognosis, reversibility, or efficacy of dopamine-targeting therapy.
studies.context: Small observational sample, exploratory correlations, and an author-disclosed pending patent application related to a long-COVID dopamine treatment require caution.
studies.disclosure: The paper reports a lead-author patent application for a rasagiline/tyramine-based long-COVID approach and other financial interests. Check the declaration in the study.

correction.summary: A published corrigendum corrected supplementary data and selected negative/exploratory analyses; authors stated primary interpretation was unchanged. Consult the updated paper and correction together.

studies.title: Senolytic therapy alleviates physiological human brain aging and COVID-19 neuropathology
studies.model: Human brain organoids, postmortem tissue and SARS-CoV-2-exposed transgenic mice
studies.observed: Senescence-associated signals appeared in infected organoids and postmortem tissue. In research models, senolytic approaches reduced some inflammatory and viral readouts; mouse experiments reported improved dopamine-neuron survival.
studies.notShown: Organoid and mouse outcomes do not prove safe senolytic treatments, reversal of established neuron dysfunction, or prevention of neurological disease in humans.
studies.context: Different models and interventions from NR-001; improvements in experimental animal outcomes are not clinical efficacy.
studies.disclosure: Interventions discussed are experimental in this context and not recommended for self-treatment.

markers.name: VMAT2 · SLC18A2
markers.role: Vesicular monoamine transporter; PET target in NR-002
markers.meaning: A proxy for aspects of monoaminergic terminal integrity, not a direct neuron count.

markers.name: α-synuclein · SNCA
markers.meaning: Gene dosage associations in an experimental model do not establish Parkinson's risk after COVID.

markers.name: Senescence-associated secretory phenotype
markers.meaning: A broad phenotype, not one protein or a single validated neuronal test.

markers.name: p16 · CDKN2A
markers.meaning: In a post-mitotic neuron, marker positivity alone is not proof of irreversible aging.

questions.title: Can living dopamine neurons regain function after a senescence-associated response?
questions.prediction: If some senescence-associated neuronal dysfunction is reversible, longitudinal models should show regained neurotransmission and normalization of multiple stress markers in viable, tracked neurons.
questions.falsifier: Persistent loss of function despite survival and resolution of stress signals, or apparent recovery explained entirely by selection of surviving healthy cells.
questions.alternative: Changes may represent transient inflammatory stress rather than stable neuronal senescence.
questions.evidenceNeeded: Track the same identified neurons over time with viability, function and multi-marker measurements; independent replication.
questions.boundary: Neither the cell-culture evidence nor the animal evidence demonstrates restoration of established senescence-associated dysfunction in a living human dopamine neuron.

questions.title: Does reduced human VMAT2 binding reflect regulation, terminal injury, or both?
questions.prediction: If VMAT2 regulation contributes independently of permanent terminal loss, longitudinal binding and complementary functional measures may recover without evidence of anatomical regrowth.
questions.falsifier: Stable binding deficits alongside independent evidence of terminal loss despite symptom changes.
questions.alternative: Differences in medication exposure, group composition or other biological factors may influence PET signals.
questions.evidenceNeeded: Replication in larger cohorts with medication controls, complementary imaging, and repeated measurements.
questions.boundary: PET binding alone cannot establish how many cells have died, whether terminal loss has occurred, or whether an individual's abnormal signal could recover.

questions.title: Are neuronal changes driven by direct infection, indirect inflammation, or both?
questions.prediction: If mechanisms differ, experiments separating direct infection and noninfectious inflammatory exposure should produce distinguishable cell-type and molecular signatures.
questions.falsifier: Comparable signatures without demonstrable neuronal infection, or signatures explained by a shared nonspecific stress response.
questions.alternative: Systemic immune, vascular, and treatment-related effects may contribute to symptoms independently of neuronal infection.
questions.evidenceNeeded: Multiple human-relevant models, carefully controlled tissue comparisons and independent clinical corroboration.
questions.boundary: Culture susceptibility cannot establish the prevalence of neuronal infection in living people or prove that direct infection explains long-COVID symptoms.

questions.title: Do preclinical improvements predict meaningful, safe human recovery?
questions.prediction: A credible clinical benefit would require controlled human evidence of improved function and acceptable safety, beyond molecular biomarker changes.
questions.falsifier: No clinically important benefit in rigorous controlled studies, or unacceptable adverse effects despite favorable biomarkers.
questions.alternative: The original lab effects may depend on viral strain, dosing context, model limitations or non-neuronal pathways.
questions.evidenceNeeded: Independent mechanistic replication, safety characterization and appropriately designed human trials by qualified researchers.
questions.boundary: None of these sources shows that a drug reverses long-COVID brain injury in humans; any experimental intervention would require independent clinical safety and efficacy evaluation.
